9.solution:
Let \(w = \dfrac{z-1}{z+1}\), noting that \(z = -1\) is excluded since it makes the denominator vanish. A complex number is purely imaginary exactly when its real part is zero, that is, when \(w + \bar{w} = 0\).

Conjugation respects quotients, so \(\bar{w} = \dfrac{\bar{z}-1}{\bar{z}+1}\) and the condition reads
\(\dfrac{z-1}{z+1} + \dfrac{\bar{z}-1}{\bar{z}+1} = 0\).

Multiply through by \((z+1)(\bar{z}+1)\), which is non-zero:
\((z-1)(\bar{z}+1) + (\bar{z}-1)(z+1) = 0\).

Expanding, the first bracket gives \(z\bar{z} + z - \bar{z} - 1\) and the second gives \(z\bar{z} - z + \bar{z} - 1\). Adding them, \(z\) cancels with \(-z\) and \(-\bar{z}\) with \(+\bar{z}\), leaving
\(2z\bar{z} - 2 = 0\), so \(z\bar{z} = 1\).

Since \(z\bar{z} = |z|^{2}\), this gives \(|z|^{2} = 1\) and therefore \(|z| = 1\).

The same conclusion in cartesian form: with \(z = x + iy\),
\(\dfrac{z-1}{z+1} = \dfrac{(x-1+iy)(x+1-iy)}{(x+1)^{2}+y^{2}} = \dfrac{\left(x^{2}+y^{2}-1\right) + 2iy}{(x+1)^{2}+y^{2}}\),
and the real part of this vanishes precisely when \(x^{2}+y^{2} = 1\), i.e. on the unit circle -- not inside it and not outside it.

The converse holds too, so the unit circle is exactly the right set: writing \(z = e^{i\theta}\) and dividing numerator and denominator by \(e^{i\theta/2}\),
\(\dfrac{e^{i\theta/2} - e^{-i\theta/2}}{e^{i\theta/2} + e^{-i\theta/2}} = \dfrac{2i\sin(\theta/2)}{2\cos(\theta/2)} = i\tan(\theta/2)\),
which is purely imaginary.

As a numerical check, \(z = i\) gives \(\dfrac{i-1}{i+1} = \dfrac{(i-1)(1-i)}{(1+i)(1-i)} = \dfrac{2i}{2} = i\), purely imaginary, and \(|i| = 1\).

So \(|z|\) is equal to 1.

110.solution:
Adding the same constant to every term of an A.P. leaves it an A.P., so add \(1\) to each of the three given terms:

\(\dfrac{a}{b+c} + 1 = \dfrac{a+b+c}{b+c}\), \(\quad \dfrac{b}{c+a} + 1 = \dfrac{a+b+c}{c+a}\), \(\quad \dfrac{c}{a+b} + 1 = \dfrac{a+b+c}{a+b}\).

Hence \(\dfrac{a+b+c}{b+c}, \dfrac{a+b+c}{c+a}, \dfrac{a+b+c}{a+b}\) are in A.P. Dividing every term by the non-zero constant \(a+b+c\) preserves the progression, so

\(\dfrac{1}{b+c}, \dfrac{1}{c+a}, \dfrac{1}{a+b}\) are in A.P.

Now apply the A.P. condition -- twice the middle term equals the sum of the outer two:
\(\dfrac{2}{c+a} = \dfrac{1}{b+c} + \dfrac{1}{a+b} = \dfrac{(a+b) + (b+c)}{(b+c)(a+b)} = \dfrac{a+2b+c}{(b+c)(a+b)}\).

Cross-multiplying,
\(2(b+c)(a+b) = (a+2b+c)(c+a)\).

The left side expands to \(2\left(ab + b^{2} + ac + bc\right) = 2ab + 2b^{2} + 2ac + 2bc\).

For the right side, group \(a+2b+c = (a+c) + 2b\), giving \((a+c)^{2} + 2b(a+c) = a^{2} + 2ac + c^{2} + 2ab + 2bc\).

Cancelling the common terms \(2ab\), \(2ac\) and \(2bc\) from both sides leaves
\(2b^{2} = a^{2} + c^{2}\),

which says exactly that \(b^{2}\) is the arithmetic mean of \(a^{2}\) and \(c^{2}\). So \(a^{2}, b^{2}, c^{2}\) are in A.P.

A concrete check that also separates this from the other choices: \(a = 1, b = 5, c = 7\) satisfies \(2(25) = 1 + 49\). The three given terms are then \(\tfrac{1}{12}, \tfrac{5}{8}, \tfrac{7}{6}\), with common difference \(\tfrac{5}{8} - \tfrac{1}{12} = \tfrac{13}{24}\) and \(\tfrac{7}{6} - \tfrac{5}{8} = \tfrac{13}{24}\) -- so they are genuinely in A.P. Yet for this triple \(1, 5, 7\) is not an A.P., is not a G.P. (\(25 \neq 7\)), and \(7, 1, 5\) is not an A.P. either. So the hypothesis forces only the relation between the squares.

113.solution:
First take the period of \(|\sin t|\). Although \(\sin t\) itself has period \(2\pi\), we have \(\sin(t + \pi) = -\sin t\), and the modulus removes that sign, so \(|\sin(t+\pi)| = |\sin t|\). Taking the modulus reflects the negative arch of the sine curve above the axis, making it a copy of the positive arch, so \(|\sin t|\) has period \(\pi\) -- half that of \(\sin t\).

Now put \(t = 2x\). The factor \(2\) compresses the graph horizontally by a factor of \(2\), so the period in \(x\) is \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

Verify directly:
\(\left|\sin 2\left(x + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right| = \left|\sin(2x + \pi)\right| = \left|-\sin 2x\right| = \left|\sin 2x\right|\)
for every \(x\), so \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) is certainly a period.

It is also the smallest one. Any period must send zeros to zeros. Here \(|\sin 2x| = 0\) exactly when \(2x\) is a multiple of \(\pi\), i.e. when \(x\) is a multiple of \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so consecutive zeros are \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) apart. If \(T\) were a period with \(0 < T < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), then from \(f(0) = 0\) we would need \(f(T) = 0\), forcing \(T\) to be a multiple of \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) -- a contradiction.

A quick check that a smaller candidate really does fail: at \(T = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\), \(f(0) = 0\) but \(f\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \left|\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right| = 1\).

Hence the period of \(|\sin 2x|\) is \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

The general rule: \(\sin kx\) has period \(\dfrac{2\pi}{|k|}\), while \(|\sin kx|\) has period \(\dfrac{\pi}{|k|}\).

116.solution:
Convert each binary numeral to base 10 by adding the place values \(8, 4, 2, 1\) wherever a \(1\) appears.

\((1010)_{2} = 1 \times 2^{3} + 0 \times 2^{2} + 1 \times 2^{1} + 0 \times 2^{0} = 8 + 0 + 2 + 0 = 10\).

\((111)_{2} = 1 \times 2^{2} + 1 \times 2^{1} + 1 \times 2^{0} = 4 + 2 + 1 = 7\).

Multiplying in base 10, \(10 \times 7 = 70\), so \(X = 70\).

As a cross-check, do the multiplication in binary and convert only at the end. Since \((111)_{2} = (100)_{2} + (10)_{2} + (1)_{2}\), the product is \(1010\) shifted left two places, plus \(1010\) shifted left one place, plus \(1010\) itself:
\(101000 + 10100 + 1010 = 1000110\).

Reading \((1000110)_{2}\) back in base 10 gives \(64 + 4 + 2 = 70\), which agrees.
